# Introduction {-}

In this notebook we use XGBoost to make predictions of RestBP from the Heart data. The theory of the model can be found in [References] [1,2,3].

# Packages {-}

Loading libraries:
```{r Load libraries, message = FALSE}
library(tidyverse) # used to manipulate data and plot
library(ISLR2) #package contains the data files, but not this one
library(ggfortify) # some extra ggplot functions
library(GGally) # pairs ggplot and other options
library(flextable) # nice displays of printed data
library(DT) #more nice table displays from RStudio
library(broom) # neat model summary
library(car) # useful tools for regression analysis
library(MASS) # for LDA analysis
library(class) # for knn analysis
library(caret) # for confusion matrix and for crossvalidation

library(xgboost)
```

# Data {-}

We import the Heart data made all numeric from the rds file created in [References] [1].

```{r}
readRDS(file="Heartall.rds")
Heartall
```

# Data Description {-}

```{r}
Heartall %>% summary
```

# Data Wrangling {-}

It's desirable to scale the data for xgboost.

```{r}
Heartall.scaled = Heartall %>% sapply(FUN = function (x) {
  (x-min(x))/(max(x)-min(x))})  %>% data.frame
Heartall.scaled %>% summary
```

#One-Hot encoding of categorical variables

Package <code>mltools</code> is best at one-hot encoding. It uses package <code>data.table</code>, which is already incorporated into tidyverse.

```{r}
library(mltools)
dfx = one_hot(as.data.table(Heart))
dfx %>% glimpse
dfx.scaled =dfx %>% sapply(FUN = function (x) {
  (x-min(x))/(max(x)-min(x))})  %>% data.frame
dfx.scaled %>% summary
```

# Research Problem {-}
We will use xgboost to predict RestBP from all the other drivers.  WE anticipate a better accuracy than the other methods. Here are the previous results.

```{r}
AccuracyComparisonAll = readRDS(file="AccuracyComparisonAll.rds")
AccuracyComparisonAll %>% mutate(Measure = "RMSE", .before=1) %>% 
  DT::datatable(caption="Accuracy Comparison, all drivers")
```


# Analysis {-}

We follow [References] [2] for the modeling.

## Preparing data for xgboost

Separate the target variable (called the label) from the others, the covariates

```{r}
Heartall.scaled_covariates = Heartall.scaled %>% select(-RestBP)
Heartall.scaled_labels = Heartall.scaled %>% select(RestBP)
```

```{r}
dfx.scaled_covariates = dfx.scaled %>% select(-RestBP)
dfx.scaled_labels = dfx.scaled %>% select(RestBP)
```

## Create data matrix

```{r}
Heartall.scaled_covariates_matrix = data.matrix(Heartall.scaled_covariates)
Heartall.scaled_labels_matrix = data.matrix(Heartall.scaled_labels)
```

```{r}
dfx.scaled_covariates_matrix = data.matrix(dfx.scaled_covariates)
dfx.scaled_labels_matrix = data.matrix(dfx.scaled_labels)
```

## Convert to Dmatrix

This step is desirable because the Dmatrix format is designed for sparse matrices.

```{r}
dheart = xgb.DMatrix(data = Heartall.scaled_covariates_matrix,
                     label = Heartall.scaled_labels_matrix)
```

```{r}
dfxheart = xgb.DMatrix(data = dfx.scaled_covariates_matrix,
                     label = dfx.scaled_labels_matrix)
```

## XGBoost run

```{r}
fit.xg.all = xgboost(data = dheart, nrounds=50,
                     max_depth=3, verbose = F)
```

```{r}
fit.xg.oh = xgboost(data = dfxheart, nrounds=50,
                     max_depth=3, verbose = F)
```

## Prediction

```{r}
pred.xg.all = predict(fit.xg.all, newdata=Heartall.scaled_covariates_matrix)
pred.xg.all.unscaled = mean(Heartall$RestBP) + pred.xg.all*sd(Heartall$RestBP)
pred.xg.all.unscaled %>% summary
```

```{r}
pred.xg.oh = predict(fit.xg.oh, newdata=dfx.scaled_covariates_matrix)
pred.xg.oh.unscaled = mean(dfx$RestBP) + pred.xg.oh*sd(dfx$RestBP)
pred.xg.oh.unscaled %>% summary
```

## Visualization

```{r}
plot.xg.all = ggplot(Heartall) +
  geom_point(aes(RestBP, pred.xg.all.unscaled))+
  geom_abline(aes(slope=1, intercept=0), color="blue", linetype="dashed", linewidth=1) +
  theme_bw() + 
  labs(title="RestBP vs Fitted Values",
       subtitle="XGBoost, all drivers",
       x="Actual RestBP (mmHg)", y="Fitted RestBP")
plot.xg.all
```

```{r}
plot.xg.oh = ggplot(dfx) +
  geom_point(aes(RestBP, pred.xg.oh.unscaled))+
  geom_abline(aes(slope=1, intercept=0), color="blue", linetype="dashed", linewidth=1) +
  theme_bw() + 
  labs(title="RestBP vs Fitted Values",
       subtitle="XGBoost, one-hot drivers",
       x="Actual RestBP (mmHg)", y="Fitted RestBP")
plot.xg.oh
```

Quite biased.

## Importance

```{r}
importance_matrix = xgb.importance(names(Heartall.scaled_covariates_matrix), 
                                   model=fit.xg.all)
importance_matrix
library(Ckmeans.1d.dp) # required for ggplot version
xgb.ggplot.importance(importance_matrix, top_n = 7) + 
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position='none')+
  geom_label(aes(label=round(importance_matrix$Gain[1:7],4)))
```

## Feature plot

We can visualize a composite of all the trees used in the model. The numbers at the leaves are the odds of arriving at that leaf.

```{r}
library(DiagrammeR) # needs to be installed for this plot.
xgb.plot.multi.trees(feature_names = names(Heartall.scaled_covariates_matrix), 
                     model = fit.xg.all, features_keep = 3)
```

```{r}
odds_to_probs <- function(odds){
    return(exp(odds)/ (1 + exp(odds)))
}

# probability of top leaf
odds_to_probs(-0.28412)
```

There is a 43% likelihood of arriving in leaf 1 averaged over all trees included in the analysis for the model.

## Accuracy

```{r}
accuracy.rmse.xg.all = ModelMetrics::rmse(pred.xg.all.unscaled, Heartall$RestBP)
accuracy.rmse.xg.all
```

The accuracy is `r accuracy.rmse.xg.all`.

```{r}
accuracy.rmse.xg.oh = ModelMetrics::rmse(pred.xg.oh.unscaled, dfx$RestBP)
accuracy.rmse.xg.oh
```

One-hot encoding helped a bit.

## Comparison

```{r}
AccuracyComparisonAll %>% 
  mutate(XGB = accuracy.rmse.xg.all %>% round(digits=4)) %>%
  mutate(XGOH = accuracy.rmse.xg.oh %>% round(digits=4)) %>% 
  mutate(Measure = "RMSE", .before=1) %>% 
  DT::datatable(caption="Accuracy Comparison, all and one-hot drivers")
```

# Conclusion {-}

This XGBoost model, one-hot encoded or not, gives results worse than regression measured by RMSE as an accuracy. It appears to be quite biased, as was a neural net and a random forest.

One-hot encoding helped, but not a lot.
